passage:
Nursery teacher's note: Omkar, age 4
Since his baby brother Tushar was born two weeks ago, Omkar has changed. He used to ask clearly for "apple juice, please". Now he says "ju-ju" and lifts his arms to be carried. He has had two toilet accidents this week, after months of none. At story time he climbs into my lap and sucks his thumb.
I haven't corrected the baby talk. I carry him when I can and tell him, "You're still my Omkar." I phoned his mother today, and we agreed on extra lap time at home and at school.

qa.q: What does Omkar now say instead of 'apple juice, please'?
qa.a: "Ju-ju".

qa.q: Why might Omkar be acting like a baby since Tushar was born?
qa.a: He may be worried there is no room left for him to be looked after, so being small is his way of asking for the care the baby gets.

qa.q: Which choice of the teacher's is most helpful, and why?
qa.a: Not correcting the baby talk and saying 'You're still my Omkar', which answers his worry directly; the plan for extra lap time at home helps too.

qa.q: How might Omkar's mother feel reading about the toilet accidents?
qa.a: She might feel worried and stretched with a newborn, but also relieved to have a simple plan for extra lap time together.

grounding: A nursery teacher notes that a four-year-old has gone back to baby talk, accidents and clinging since his brother's birth, and responds with closeness instead of correction.

In their village near Dharwad, Jyoti had been proud of going to the latrine by herself and of saying long words like "aeroplane". Then baby Rehana came home. Now Jyoti, five, crawled on the floor, said "mama-mama", and wanted her milk fed with a spoon, like the baby. She wet her frock twice in one day. She clung to Avva's sari and cried whenever Avva put her down.
Avva laughed softly, picked her up with one arm and held the baby with the other. "Two babies today," she said, and gave Jyoti a spoonful of milk. Jyoti giggled.

qa.q: What did Jyoti say instead of long words like 'aeroplane'?
qa.a: "Mama-mama".

qa.q: What might Jyoti be feeling when she cries whenever Avva puts her down?
qa.a: She may be afraid the new baby has taken her place and wants to check there is still room for her in Avva's arms.

qa.q: What choice did Avva make, and why does it help?
qa.a: She picked Jyoti up alongside the baby and fed her a spoonful without scolding, which shows Jyoti she is still cared for.

qa.q: What would change if Avva had told Jyoti to stop acting like a baby?
qa.a: Jyoti would likely feel pushed away and cling even harder, because her worry about losing her place would grow.

grounding: A five-year-old in a village goes back to baby talk, accidents and clinging after her sister is born, and Avva answers with warmth.

In their flat in Addis Ababa, Esther, who was five, had been dressing herself and chatting in whole sentences for a year. Then her brother Abebe was born. Now she lay on the rug beside his basket, kicking her legs. "Me baby too," she said in a squeaky voice. She asked for her old bottle from the cupboard. When their mother fed Abebe, Esther pressed against her side and wouldn't move.
Her father knelt down. "Shall I carry my big baby to the window to see the birds?" Esther nodded hard and held on tight.

qa.q: What did Esther say in a squeaky voice?
qa.a: "Me baby too."

qa.q: Why does Esther press against her mother's side while Abebe is being fed?
qa.a: She seems to worry the baby is getting all the care, and staying close checks that there is still room for her.

qa.q: What choice did Esther's father make, and why does it help?
qa.a: He offered to carry his 'big baby' to the window without mocking her, giving her the closeness she was asking for. 🤍

qa.q: How might Esther's mother feel with Esther pressed against her during feeds?
qa.a: She may feel stretched and tired, but also understand that Esther needs extra closeness right now.

grounding: A five-year-old in Addis Ababa returns to baby talk and her old bottle after her brother is born, asking in her own way to be looked after too.

In the clinic waiting room, Ammi held baby Salma, who was there for her first injection. Kiran, five, who usually read the posters aloud, climbed onto the bench and tugged Ammi's dupatta. "Kiki up. Kiki baby too," he said in a tiny voice. That morning he had wet his shorts, the first time in two years.
When the nurse smiled at Salma, Kiran crawled under the bench and whimpered.
Ammi shifted the baby to one arm and patted her lap. "Room for two," she said. Kiran climbed up, tucked his head under her chin, and went quiet.

qa.q: Why was baby Salma at the clinic?
qa.a: Salma was there for her first injection.

qa.q: What might Kiran want when he says "Kiki baby too"?
qa.a: Kiran seems to feel left out now that baby Salma gets so much care, and wants to check there is still room for him to be looked after.

qa.q: Which choice by Ammi reassured Kiran?
qa.a: Ammi shifted the baby to one arm and made room on her lap, showing him without words that there was space for both.

qa.q: How might the nurse see Kiran crawling under the bench?
qa.a: The nurse might recognise an older child feeling pushed aside by the new baby, rather than just a naughty one, and give Ammi a moment to comfort him.

grounding: Shows a five-year-old who had been dry and speaking well slipping into baby talk and clinging at the clinic after his sister's birth, asking whether he is still cared for.

I'm Lakshmi aunty from across the corridor. Bidisha, five, used to ring my bell every evening to sing me the alphabet song and tell me she'd gone to the toilet "all by myself".
Since her baby brother came home three weeks ago, she's different. Yesterday she pointed at my biscuit tin and said, "Bidu want bic-bic," in a baby voice. She wanted to be carried up the stairs. Her mother told me she'd had two accidents at night.
I don't know what's in her head. But when I sat her on my lap and said, "You're my big Bidisha and my little Bidisha," she didn't want to get down for a long time.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say when she pointed at the biscuit tin?
qa.a: "Bidu want bic-bic."

qa.q: Why might Bidisha want to be carried up the stairs again?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel left out now that her baby brother gets so much care, so being carried again checks whether she can still be looked after like a little one.

qa.q: What in Lakshmi aunty's response could help Bidisha most?
qa.a: Calling her both big and little Bidisha, without mocking the baby voice, told her she didn't have to choose between growing up and being cared for.

qa.q: What might Bidisha's mother be feeling, with a new baby and night-time accidents?
qa.a: She is likely tired and stretched thin and a bit worried about Bidisha, which may be why she mentioned it to a neighbour.

grounding: Illustrates, through a neighbour's eyes, a five-year-old who returns to baby talk and wanting to be carried after a brother's birth, seeking reassurance that she is still looked after.
